findings.mechanism: The token verification always returns true because SHA‑256 always yields a 32‑byte digest, so the length check passes for any input. This defeats authentication, allowing any caller to obtain search results (reference 01-authn-authz-and-idor).
findings.remediation: Replace the custom verify_token with proper token validation (e.g., HMAC verification against a secret key or JWT signature check) and remove the length‑only check.
findings.arithmetic: SHA‑256 output length is fixed at 32 bytes. The loop hashes the input _ROUNDS times but never changes the digest size, so len(digest)==32 is always true regardless of the supplied token.

findings.mechanism: The endpoint performs a deliberately expensive key‑stretching hash (60 000 SHA‑256 rounds) on every request without any rate‑limiting. With a single worker this caps throughput at roughly 83 req/s; higher request rates saturate the worker, causing denial‑of‑service (reference 01-authn-authz-and-idor).
findings.remediation: Remove the unnecessary key‑stretching or replace it with a fast, constant‑time token verification and add rate‑limiting (e.g., 10 req/s per client).
findings.arithmetic: Assuming one SHA‑256 takes ~0.2 µs, 60 000 rounds ≈12 ms CPU time per request. One worker can handle ~1000 ms/12 ms ≈83 requests per second. At 100 rps the worker is fully occupied, yielding worker_saturation = 1.
